items.title: Shop receipt
items.intro: A customer buys three shirts at S$19.90 and two pairs of socks at S$4.50. The till adds 9% GST. Work out what the card terminal charges.

recap.title: Receipt rung up
recap.subtitle: Floats, GST as a multiplier, and the order of discounts and tax.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: Three shirts at S$19.90. What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: 19.9 has no exact binary form, so the product prints as 59.699999999999996.
questions.takeaway: So: money stored as floats picks up tiny errors.
questions.hint_before_check: Can binary store 19.9 exactly?

code_note.title: Floats
code_note.text: Decimal numbers are stored in binary, which cannot hold most of them exactly.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Point-of-sale and accounting systems total millions of line items a day; knowing where float errors come from is why finance code rounds at the right moment or counts in cents.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the total

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

options.feedback: print() shows every digit Python stores.
print() does not add a trailing zero.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Add 9% GST to the whole basket
questions.explanation_after_check: Multiplying by 1.09 keeps 100% of the price and adds 9%: 74.88.
questions.takeaway: So: a percentage rise is a multiplier.
questions.hint_before_check: What does 1.09 represent for a price?

code_note.title: Multipliers
code_note.text: A percentage change can be written as one number to multiply by.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Tax rules change: in code, the 9% lives in one place, and every price in the catalogue updates with one edit, which a spreadsheet of hand-typed totals cannot promise.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the total

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

options.feedback: That adds S$1.09: 69.79.
That removes GST from a price that never had it: 63.03.
A power grows far too fast: 100.53.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The basket is charged S$687. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: 9% is 9 out of 100, so the GST is the subtotal × 9 / 100: S$6.18, total 74.88.
questions.takeaway: So: a percentage needs its / 100.
questions.hint_before_check: 9 what?

code_note.title: Percentages
code_note.text: A percentage is a number out of 100.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: A wrong rate on one till line is a refund queue; in a script it is one line to fix, and a test can check every rate before the store opens.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the total

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

b.feedback: // throws the cents away: 74.7, short by 18 cents.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.30000000000000004, so == 0.3 fails; rounded to cents, it matches.
questions.takeaway: So: compare money after rounding.
questions.next_bridge: fix the order of a voucher and GST.
questions.hint_before_check: Compare the exact stored value with the rounded one.

code_note.title: Comparing floats
code_note.text: == asks for an exact match, digit for digit.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Reconciliation scripts compare thousands of totals; comparing raw floats would flag matching accounts as broken.

picture.label: Calculator: the display shows the sum

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

options.label: True True
options.feedback: The stored sum is a hair above 0.3.

options.label: False False
options.feedback: Rounding to 2 places removes the error.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The S$10 voucher should come off before GST. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Line 2 already added GST, so a S$10 voucher taken before GST is worth S$10.90 here: 98.1.
questions.takeaway: So: the order of operations is the order of the business rule.
questions.hint_before_check: By the time line 3 runs, what does price already include?

code_note.title: Order of steps
code_note.text: Each line works on what the lines before it produced.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Discount-then-tax rules decide what a customer pays; encoding them once in code applies the same rule at every till.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the total

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

items.title: Making change
items.intro: A customer pays S$100 for a S$63.45 bill. The change is S$36.55, or 3655 cents. Count it into notes and coins.

recap.title: Change counted
recap.subtitle: // and %, cents as whole numbers, and remainders that surprise.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: How many S$10 notes, and what is left?
questions.explanation_after_check: // counts whole S$10 notes (1000 cents each): 3. % keeps the cents left over: 655.
questions.takeaway: So: // counts, % remains.
questions.hint_before_check: One operator counts whole notes, the other keeps what is left.

code_note.title: Floor division
code_note.text: One operator gives whole units, another gives what is left.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Cash-handling and ATM software splits amounts into notes this way, thousands of times a day, without a cashier counting.

picture.label: Change: S$10 notes and S$1 coins

assets.motion: notes fly from the pile into a fan, then coins drop onto stacks one by one

options.feedback: // gives a whole number.
% gives the remaining cents.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Take out one S$5 note
questions.explanation_after_check: // gives 1 whole S$5 note, leaving 155 cents.
questions.takeaway: So: // for whole units.
questions.hint_before_check: How many whole S$5 notes fit?

code_note.title: Whole units
code_note.text: Some quantities only come in whole pieces.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: The same split drives payroll in cash, coin orders for banks and change machines.

picture.label: Change: S$10 notes and S$1 coins

assets.motion: notes fly from the pile into a fan, then coins drop onto stacks one by one

options.feedback: A fraction of a note: 1.31.
That is the leftover, not the count: 155.
That multiplies: 327500.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The change comes out one cent short. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: (100 − 63.45) × 100 is 3654.9999999999995, and int() cuts the decimals off: 3654. round() goes to the nearest cent: 3655.
questions.takeaway: So: round, never cut, when turning money into cents.
questions.hint_before_check: What does int() do to 3654.9999999999995?

code_note.title: int() cuts
code_note.text: Converting to a whole number drops the decimals without rounding.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: A cent lost per transaction is thousands of dollars a year at scale; finance code converts to cents with rounding, then works in whole numbers.

questions.scene_label: A cent lost to a float.

picture.label: Change: S$10 notes and S$1 coins

assets.motion: notes fly from the pile into a fan, then coins drop onto stacks one by one

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: A refund makes the amount negative. What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: Python's % takes the sign of the divisor: −7 % 3 is 2, and 7 % −3 is −2.
questions.takeaway: So: check remainders on negative amounts.
questions.hint_before_check: % follows the sign of the number you divide by.

code_note.title: Negative remainders
code_note.text: Languages disagree about remainders of negative numbers.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Refunds and reversals are negative; code ported from Excel or Java can split them differently in Python.

picture.label: Calculator

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

options.feedback: That is how C and Java behave, not Python.
The signs follow the divisor.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Split 155 cents into 50-cent coins. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: After taking out three 50-cent coins, left should hold the remainder: 155 % 50 = 5.
questions.takeaway: So: // for the count, % for what is left.
questions.hint_before_check: After counting the coins, what should left hold?

code_note.title: Pairs
code_note.text: // and % answer the two halves of one division.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Coin-counting and cash-recycling machines run exactly this loop for every denomination.

picture.label: Change: S$10 notes and S$1 coins

assets.motion: notes fly from the pile into a fan, then coins drop onto stacks one by one

items.title: Profit margin
items.intro: Last quarter the café chain took S$250,000 in revenue and spent S$190,000. Work out the profit margin, then check a markup.

recap.title: Margin worked out
recap.subtitle: Brackets, margin against markup, powers and percentage change.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: / runs before −, so this is 250000 − 0.76: 249999.24.
questions.takeaway: So: without brackets, Python divides first.
questions.hint_before_check: Which operator runs first?

code_note.title: Precedence
code_note.text: Multiplication and division run before addition and subtraction.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Finance teams rebuild margin reports every month; a formula written once in code is checked once, instead of retyped into hundreds of cells.

picture.label: Calculator: the display shows the result

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

options.feedback: That would need brackets around revenue − cost.
Nothing here multiplies by 100.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Profit margin as a percentage
questions.explanation_after_check: Profit, 60000, as a share of revenue is 0.24: 24.0%.
questions.takeaway: So: margin = profit / revenue.
questions.hint_before_check: Profit as a share of revenue.

code_note.title: Shares
code_note.text: A share is a part divided by the whole.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Margins are compared across hundreds of outlets; code computes every one the same way from the raw ledger.

picture.label: Calculator: the display shows the result

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

options.feedback: // floors 0.24 to 0: 0.
That multiplies: 1500000000000.
A remainder, not a share: 6000000.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The S$80 bag's margin should be 0.25. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Dividing by cost gives the markup, 0.333. Margin divides by the selling price: 0.25.
questions.takeaway: So: margin uses price, markup uses cost.
questions.hint_before_check: Margin and markup divide by different things.

code_note.title: Two ratios
code_note.text: The same profit divided by different bases gives different answers.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Mixing up margin and markup misprices whole product ranges; naming each in code makes the difference explicit.

questions.scene_label: A markup reported as a margin.

picture.label: Calculator: the display shows the result

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

b.feedback: Still the markup, now as a percentage: 33.3.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: ** runs right to left: 2 ** (3 ** 2) is 2 ** 9, 512. With brackets, 8 ** 2 is 64.
questions.takeaway: So: chained powers group from the right.
questions.hint_before_check: Which ** runs first in a chain?

code_note.title: Powers
code_note.text: Powers group differently from other operators.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Growth over several periods is a power; a misplaced bracket turns a 3-year projection into nonsense.

picture.label: Calculator: the display shows the result

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

options.feedback: Without brackets the right-hand power runs first.
The order is the other way round.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Sales fell from S$120k to S$90k: −25%. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: Without brackets, Python works out 90 − (120 / 120 × 100) = −10. Bracketing the difference gives (90 − 120) / 120 × 100 = −25.0.
questions.takeaway: So: bracket the difference first.
questions.hint_before_check: Which part should be divided by the old value?

code_note.title: Brackets
code_note.text: Brackets decide what is divided.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Percentage changes drive dashboards and board reports; a plausible but wrong −10% is more dangerous than an obvious error.

picture.label: Calculator: the display shows the result

assets.motion: keys glow one after another as the body dips with each press, then the display counts up

items.title: Compound interest
items.intro: A customer saves S$1,000 at 3% a year for 10 years, and the interest is added each year. Grow it with Python.

recap.title: Savings grown
recap.subtitle: Powers, brackets, compounding periods and rates as decimals.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: S$1,000 at 3% for two years. What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: 1.03 ** 2 is 1.0609 in decimal but not exactly in binary, so the result prints as 1060.8999999999999.
questions.takeaway: So: format money before showing it.
questions.hint_before_check: 1.03 is a decimal too.

code_note.title: Recap
code_note.text: Floats print every stored digit.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Banks compound millions of accounts; the same formula in code runs for all of them, and rounding rules are applied in one place.

picture.label: Piggy bank: one coin for each S$50 of interest

assets.motion: coins fall one at a time, turn edge-on and vanish at the slot line; the pig squashes and wobbles per coin; a bounce option sends the coin off the pig

options.feedback: print() shows the full float.
The interest on interest is only 90 cents.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: Grow S$1,000 for ten years
questions.explanation_after_check: (1 + r) ** n applies the 3% growth ten times, each on the new balance: 1343.92.
questions.takeaway: So: ** compounds.
questions.hint_before_check: The growth multiplies once a year, ten times.

code_note.title: Compounding
code_note.text: Repeated growth is a power.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Savings calculators, loan schedules and pension projections all reuse this one line.

picture.label: Piggy bank: one coin for each S$50 of interest

assets.motion: coins fall one at a time, turn edge-on and vanish at the slot line; the pig squashes and wobbles per coin; a bounce option sends the coin off the pig

options.feedback: Ten times the balance: 10300.0.
^ is not a power in Python: TypeError.
Floor division: 103.0.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: Ten years of saving shows no interest. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: ** runs first, so r ** n is 0.03 to the 10th, almost 0: the balance stays at 1000. Bracketing 1 + r compounds it: 1343.92.
questions.takeaway: So: bracket the growth factor.
questions.hint_before_check: What is r ** n for r = 0.03?

code_note.title: Recap
code_note.text: Powers run before multiplication and addition.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Missing compounding understates a 30-year pension by tens of thousands; code reviews catch it once, for every customer.

picture.label: Piggy bank: one coin for each S$50 of interest

assets.motion: coins fall one at a time, turn edge-on and vanish at the slot line; the pig squashes and wobbles per coin; a bounce option sends the coin off the pig

b.feedback: Interest on the deposit only, no compounding: 1300.0.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: Interest added monthly instead. What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: 120 monthly steps of 0.25% grow slightly more than 10 yearly steps of 3%: 1349.35.
questions.takeaway: So: compounding more often earns more.
questions.hint_before_check: More frequent compounding.

code_note.title: Periods
code_note.text: The rate and the number of periods must match.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Comparing a monthly and a yearly product is one change to two numbers in code.

picture.label: Piggy bank: one coin for each S$50 of interest

assets.motion: coins fall one at a time, turn edge-on and vanish at the slot line; the pig squashes and wobbles per coin; a bounce option sends the coin off the pig

options.feedback: That is yearly compounding.
That is one year of interest.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The savings grow to over S$1 billion. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: With rate = 3, the balance quadruples every year: 1048576000. 3% is 3 / 100: 1343.92.
questions.takeaway: So: rates go in as decimals.
questions.hint_before_check: How is 3% written as a decimal?

code_note.title: Units
code_note.text: A percentage and a decimal differ by a factor of 100.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Rates often arrive as percentages from data feeds; converting them in one place avoids a 100× error everywhere.

items.title: Order form
items.intro: Customers type quantities and budgets into an order form. Everything typed reaches Python as text. Turn it into numbers safely.

recap.title: Order taken
recap.subtitle: input() as text, conversions, types and == against =: the phase together.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: * repeats text, so "3" * 2 is "33".
questions.takeaway: So: text from a form must be converted before maths.
questions.hint_before_check: What does * do to text?

code_note.title: Text and numbers
code_note.text: The same symbol does different things to text and numbers.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Order forms, CSV exports and bank feeds all deliver numbers as text; every finance script starts by converting them.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the order

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

options.feedback: qty is text, not a number.
print() shows text without quotes.

questions.label: Fill
questions.ask: The customer types 3. Double the order
questions.explanation_after_check: int() turns the text "3" into the number 3: 6.
questions.takeaway: So: convert input before calculating.
questions.hint_before_check: Quantities are whole numbers.

code_note.title: Converting
code_note.text: int(), float() and str() turn values into other types.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Quantities are counts, prices are decimals; choosing the right conversion keeps an order of 3 from becoming 33.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the order

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

options.label: float
options.feedback: That gives 6.0, a float.

options.label: str
options.feedback: Still text: 33.

options.label: type
options.feedback: type() gives the type, not a number: TypeError.

questions.label: Fix
questions.ask: The customer types 500, and Python stops. Fix it.
questions.explanation_after_check: input() returns text, and Python will not compare a number with text. float() turns "500" into 500.0: True.
questions.takeaway: So: convert every input.
questions.hint_before_check: What type does input() return?

code_note.title: Recap
code_note.text: Numbers and text cannot be compared.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Comparing text instead of numbers lets "89.9" look larger than "500"; finance code converts first.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the order

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

b.feedback: Text against text compares letters: "89.9" < "500" is False.
Still a number against text: TypeError.

questions.label: Predict
questions.ask: What prints?
questions.explanation_after_check: 19.9 × 2 is a float, and "19.9" is text, so its type is str.
questions.takeaway: So: type() shows what a value is.
questions.hint_before_check: What type is 39.8?

code_note.title: Types
code_note.text: type() reports what kind of value something is.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: When imported data misbehaves, checking types is the first thing an analyst does.

picture.label: Card terminal: the screen shows the order

assets.motion: card arcs in and taps the screen (contactless rings), the terminal dips, the screen counts up, then the receipt feeds out of the top; a declined option shakes and prints nothing

options.label: <class 'int'> True

code_note.text: One = stores, two compare.

science_note.title: Why Python here
science_note.text: Payment matching runs on every transaction; one wrong symbol can stop a whole reconciliation job.
